# Production Runbook — Garment Sourcing Marketplace
**Owner after handover:** Dev A & Dev B (Laravel developers)
**Last updated by outgoing DevOps engineer:** [date]
**Architecture is frozen for 6 months:** two Hetzner VMs (app-1, db-1), no Kubernetes, no managed DB, no PaaS, no new cloud. **No new paid tools are introduced in this runbook** — everything below uses what is already installed: nginx, PHP-FPM, Supervisor, MySQL 8, certbot, cron, rclone, Backblaze B2, Uptime Kuma, Telegram, Hetzner's included support.

---

## 0. How to use this document

- Read Section 3 (Golden Rules) before touching anything.
- Section 4–6 are your recurring checklist. Do them on a schedule, not "when you remember."
- Section 8 is "something is broken" — find the matching symptom, follow it top to bottom, stop where it tells you to stop.
- Every playbook ends with **"Success looks like"** and **"Escalate if."** If you hit the escalate condition, stop — do not keep improvising on production.
- Keep a one-line **Ops Log** (shared Google Doc, free) for every change: date, who, what, why. This is not optional — it's how the next person (including future-you) understands what state the system is in.

---

## 1. Architecture at a glance

```
Internet
   │
   ▼
app-1 (Hetzner, Singapore)
  - nginx  (TLS via Let's Encrypt/certbot)
  - php8.2-fpm (Laravel 10)
  - Supervisor → queue worker process
  - Uptime Kuma (monitors app-1, db-1, public URL) → alerts Telegram group
   │  MySQL protocol, private network
   ▼
db-1 (Hetzner, Singapore)
  - MySQL 8.0
  - cron → nightly mysqldump → rclone → Backblaze B2 (14-day retention)
```

Nothing here changes. Your job is to keep these exact pieces running, not to improve them.

---

## 2. Access, credentials, secrets

Before departure, the following was done (verify these are true on your first day of ownership):

- [ ] Both devs have **personal** sudo-capable Linux users on app-1 and db-1 (not shared "root" logins), each with their own SSH key.
- [ ] The outgoing engineer's SSH key has been **removed** from `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys` and both devs' `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on both servers.
- [ ] All shared secrets live in a **free Bitwarden organization vault** (or equivalent you already use): MySQL root password, app DB user password, Hetzner Cloud account login + API token, Backblaze B2 account login + application key, domain registrar login, Telegram bot token.
- [ ] `/var/www/app/.env` is backed up to the vault as a file attachment (it contains `APP_KEY`, DB credentials — losing it without a copy means you can't decrypt existing encrypted DB columns/sessions).
- [ ] Hetzner and Backblaze billing is on a payment method **the company**, not the departing engineer, controls. Confirm auto-pay is on — a lapsed card silently kills your backups and your servers.

**If you can't find a credential**, check the vault first. If it's genuinely missing, that's an escalation (Section 10), not a guess-and-reset situation on a production password.

---

## 3. The five golden rules

1. **Never work as `root` directly.** Use your personal user + `sudo`. This keeps an audit trail (`/var/log/auth.log`).
2. **Before any change** that touches production data/config: note it in the Ops Log first, including what you expect to happen.
3. **One person touches production at a time.** Post "starting work on app-1" / "done" in the Telegram group so you don't collide.
4. **If you're not sure what a command does, don't run it on production.** Look it up, ask the other dev, or escalate. There is no "undo" on a `DROP DATABASE`.
5. **A backup you have never restored is not a backup.** Do the monthly drill in Section 9 — no exceptions.

---

## 4. Daily checks (5 minutes, every morning)

1. Open Uptime Kuma dashboard (`https://<app-1-ip-or-domain>:3001`, or wherever it's exposed). All monitors should be **green**.
2. Check the Telegram alert group for anything overnight. If there's a red alert, go to Section 8 and find the matching playbook — don't just acknowledge and move on.
3. Quick resource check:
   ```
   ssh dev@app-1 "df -h; free -h"
   ssh dev@db-1  "df -h; free -h"
   ```
   Any filesystem over 80%? → Section 8.3.

---

## 5. Weekly checks (20 minutes, every Monday)

```bash
# Certificate expiry
ssh dev@app-1 "sudo certbot certificates"
# Expect: VALID, 30+ days remaining. If under 15 days and auto-renew hasn't fired → Section 8.4

# Backup presence - last 7 days should be there
ssh dev@db-1 "rclone ls b2:<bucket-name>/db-backups/ | tail -10"
# Compare dates: should be one file per day, no gaps, sizes roughly similar to each other

# Service health
ssh dev@app-1 "sudo systemctl status nginx php8.2-fpm supervisor --no-pager"
ssh dev@db-1  "sudo systemctl status mysql --no-pager"
# All should say "active (running)"

# Queue worker
ssh dev@app-1 "sudo supervisorctl status"
# Should say RUNNING, uptime should roughly match last deploy time
```

---

## 6. Monthly checks (1 hour, first Monday of the month)

```bash
# OS security patches - do this at low-traffic hours (check analytics for your quiet window)
ssh dev@app-1 "sudo apt update && sudo apt list --upgradable"
ssh dev@db-1  "sudo apt update && sudo apt list --upgradable"

# Apply patches
sudo apt upgrade -y
# If kernel updated, a reboot is needed - schedule it, warn the team first
sudo reboot   # only if "upgradable" list showed a linux-image package

# After reboot, confirm everything came back:
sudo systemctl status nginx php8.2-fpm mysql supervisor --no-pager
```

Also this month: run the **full restore drill** (Section 9). This is the single most important monthly task — more important than patching.

Check for brute-force attempts:
```bash
sudo grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | tail -20
```
A handful is normal internet noise. Hundreds from one IP → consider `sudo ufw status` to confirm only ports 22/80/443 are open, and if `fail2ban` is installed, confirm it's active: `sudo systemctl status fail2ban`.

---

## 7. Deploying application changes

```bash
ssh dev@app-1
cd /var/www/app

php artisan down --retry=60          # put site in maintenance mode (skip for tiny changes, but prefer this for safety)

git pull origin main
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php artisan migrate --force          # only if there are new migrations
php artisan config:cache
php artisan route:cache
php artisan view:cache

sudo systemctl reload php8.2-fpm
sudo supervisorctl restart laravel-worker:*    # queue workers cache code in memory - ALWAYS restart after a deploy, even if you forgot to and nothing looks wrong yet

php artisan up
```

**Success looks like:** homepage and a couple of key pages load, `curl -I https://yourdomain.com` returns `200`, Uptime Kuma stays green, no new errors in `tail -f storage/logs/laravel.log` for a couple of minutes after deploy.

**Rollback if something's wrong:**
```bash
git log --oneline -5           # find previous commit/tag
git checkout <previous-commit>
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
# Only run migrate:rollback if the new migration is reversible AND you're sure no new data depends on the new columns.
# If in doubt about rolling back a migration, leave the schema as-is and just roll back the code - don't rollback a migration on a guess.
sudo systemctl reload php8.2-fpm
sudo supervisorctl restart laravel-worker:*
```
**Escalate if:** rollback doesn't fix it, or the migration already ran and can't be safely reversed and data looks wrong — stop, go to Section 10.

---

## 8. Incident playbooks

### 8.1 Site unreachable / 502 or 503

**Symptoms:** Uptime Kuma red, browser shows 502/503.
```bash
ssh dev@app-1
sudo systemctl status nginx php8.2-fpm --no-pager
sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/nginx/error.log
sudo tail -n 100 /var/www/app/storage/logs/laravel.log
```
- If `php8.2-fpm` is not running: `sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm`
- If nginx config was edited and is broken: `sudo nginx -t` (fix reported line, then) `sudo systemctl reload nginx`

**Success:** `curl -I https://yourdomain.com` → `200`, Uptime Kuma green.
**Escalate if:** restart doesn't fix it within 15 minutes, or the error log shows something you don't recognize (not a normal Laravel exception).

### 8.2 Database down / connection refused

```bash
ssh dev@db-1
sudo systemctl status mysql --no-pager
sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/mysql/error.log
df -h
```
- If disk is full → go to 8.3 first, then retry starting MySQL.
- If plain crash with a clean error log: `sudo systemctl restart mysql`

**Success:** `sudo mysqladmin status` shows uptime, app pages that query the DB load correctly.

**Escalate immediately, do not attempt repair yourself if:**
- error log mentions **corruption** ("InnoDB: Database page corruption", "Table ... is marked as crashed") — this is a data-loss risk. Stop. Prepare to restore from the latest good backup (Section 9) and escalate per Section 10 before doing anything destructive.

### 8.3 Disk full

```bash
df -h
sudo du -sh /var/log/* /var/www/app/storage/logs/* /var/lib/mysql/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20
```
Usual suspects: an unrotated `laravel.log`, MySQL binary logs, or old dump files left on db-1 before upload.

```bash
# Laravel log - only if it's enormous and rotation isn't configured
sudo truncate -s 0 /var/www/app/storage/logs/laravel.log

# MySQL binary logs - safe to purge, backups use mysqldump, not binlog replication
mysql -u root -p -e "PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE NOW();"

# Stray local dump files on db-1 that should've been deleted after upload
ls -la /path/to/local/backup/dir
```

**Success:** `df -h` shows the partition back under 80%.
**Escalate if:** you can't identify what's consuming the space, or it's inside `/var/lib/mysql/` and you're not sure it's safe to touch — don't delete MySQL data files guessing.

### 8.4 TLS certificate expired or renewal failing

```bash
sudo certbot certificates
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
sudo tail -50 /var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log
sudo ufw status          # ports 80 and 443 must be allowed, renewal uses port 80
```
```bash
sudo certbot renew
sudo systemctl reload nginx
```
**Success:** `sudo certbot certificates` shows VALID with 60+ days (fresh renewal), site loads with no browser warning.
**Escalate if:** renewal keeps failing and the certificate has **under 5 days** left — this breaks the site and any API integrations for customers. Treat as urgent same-day.

### 8.5 Nightly backup missing or failed

```bash
ssh dev@db-1
# Find the cron job and its log
sudo crontab -l -u root        # or whichever user owns it - check /etc/cron.d/ too
grep -i mysqldump /var/log/syslog | tail -20
rclone ls b2:<bucket-name>/db-backups/ | tail -5     # is today's file there, reasonable size?
```
Run the backup manually and watch the output:
```bash
sudo /usr/local/bin/backup-db.sh   # confirm actual path from the crontab entry
```
Common causes: B2 application key rotated/expired, disk full on db-1 (see 8.3), `rclone.conf` corrupted.

**Success:** a new dump appears in the bucket, roughly the expected size (compare to the last few days — a sudden drop to near-zero bytes means the dump itself failed, not just the upload).
**Escalate if:** you can't restore a working nightly backup within the same day. Going more than ~48 hours without a successful backup should be treated as an active incident, not a backlog item.

### 8.6 Queue jobs not processing

```bash
sudo supervisorctl status
sudo tail -100 /var/www/app/storage/logs/worker.log
sudo supervisorctl restart laravel-worker:*
free -h       # check for memory exhaustion
```
**Reminder:** workers hold old code in memory. If jobs are failing right after a deploy with "class not found"-type errors, you likely forgot to restart the worker — do it now.

**Success:** `supervisorctl status` shows RUNNING, the pending job count (check `failed_jobs` table / your queue dashboard if you have one) stops growing.
**Escalate if:** the worker keeps crash-looping on restart and the stack trace is inside vendor/framework code you don't recognize.

### 8.7 Server completely unresponsive, SSH hangs

1. Log into the **Hetzner Cloud Console** (web UI, not SSH) → select the server → open the browser-based **Console** (VNC) to see what's on screen.
2. Check the CPU/network graphs in the console for a spike (runaway process, disk I/O storm).
3. If genuinely frozen: Console → **Power → Reset**. Wait 2 minutes, retry SSH.
4. Once back in, verify everything auto-started:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl status nginx php8.2-fpm mysql supervisor --no-pager
   ```

**Success:** SSH works, all services active, Uptime Kuma green.
**Escalate if:** reset doesn't bring it back, or the console shows filesystem errors / kernel panic messages. Open a **Hetzner support ticket** (free, included with your server plan, via the Cloud Console) immediately — this is infrastructure-level, not something to debug yourselves.

### 8.8 Suspected security incident (defacement, unknown admin account, ransom note, unexplained outbound traffic)

**STOP. Do not try to clean this up alone.**

1. Limit damage without destroying evidence: `sudo systemctl stop nginx` on app-1 takes the site offline without wiping anything.
2. Take a Hetzner **snapshot** of the current (compromised) state for later investigation, and note timestamps in the Ops Log.
3. This is the one scenario where the "zero additional spend" constraint is explicitly overridden — a security incident is a business-continuity emergency, not routine ops. Escalate same-hour to company leadership to approve emergency contractor help (Section 10). If customer data may have been exposed, leadership also needs to loop in legal counsel regarding notification obligations.

---

## 9. Backup verification & restore drill (do monthly, no exceptions)

**Do this on db-1 into a throwaway database — never restore over the production database during a drill.**

```bash
ssh dev@db-1
mkdir -p ~/restore-drill && cd ~/restore-drill

rclone copy b2:<bucket-name>/db-backups/<latest-file>.sql.gz .
gunzip <latest-file>.sql.gz

mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE restore_test;"
mysql -u root -p restore_test < <latest-file>.sql

# Sanity-check: row count and recency, using a table you know is written to daily
mysql -u root -p restore_test -e "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;"
mysql -u root -p restore_test -e "SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM orders;"

# Cleanup
mysql -u root -p -e "DROP DATABASE restore_test;"
rm -rf ~/restore-drill
```

**Success:** restore completes with no SQL errors, row count is in the right ballpark vs. production, and the most recent row's timestamp is within the last 24–48 hours.

**Escalate / flag as an incident if:** the restore fails, or the data is stale — that means recent nightly backups have silently not been working even though cron reported success. Treat it exactly like Section 8.5.

### Real disaster recovery (actual data loss, not a drill)

1. `php artisan down` on app-1.
2. Before touching the existing (possibly bad) database, take a safety dump of its current state anyway: `mysqldump -u root -p production_db > /tmp/pre-restore-safety-copy.sql`.
3. Restore the latest good backup into the real `production_db` (or a freshly created one, then repoint `.env` if the name changes).
4. `php artisan up`, spot-check the site manually.
5. Write a full timeline in the Ops Log: what was lost, what window of data is gone, what you did. Tell management — customers may need to be told some recent orders/changes were lost.

---

## 10. Escalation matrix — when to stop touching it

| Situation | Who / What | How |
|---|---|---|
| VM frozen, kernel/filesystem errors, network issue at the host level | Hetzner Support (free, included with your plan) | Open a ticket from the Cloud Console, reference your project/server ID |
| MySQL reports corruption, or you're not sure data is intact | Stop immediately, don't "try fixes." Restore from backup (Section 9) | Escalate to management if the restore itself doesn't fully resolve it or data loss window is unclear |
| You've spent 30+ minutes on an outage with no clear next step and the site is still down | Don't keep guessing on production | Pull in the other developer to pair; if still stuck, escalate to management |
| Security incident of any kind | Treat as emergency, explicit exception to zero-spend rule | Notify company leadership same-hour for approval of emergency contractor/legal help; isolate the server first (Section 8.8) |
| Backup unavailable/broken for more than 48 hours | Active incident, not backlog | Fix same-day; if blocked (e.g., Backblaze account locked), escalate to whoever controls company billing |
| A command you don't understand looks like the "fix" | Don't run it | Ask the other dev first; if still unsure, don't run it on production at all |

**Pre-arranged contacts (fill in before departure):**
- Hetzner Support: via console.hetzner.cloud → Support ticket
- Backblaze B2 account owner / billing contact: ______
- Company director/owner authorized to approve emergency spend: ______ (phone)
- Domain registrar login holder: ______

---

## 11. Pre-departure checklist (completed before last day)

- [ ] Individual sudo users + SSH keys created for both devs on app-1 and db-1; departing engineer's access removed last.
- [ ] Shared password vault populated (MySQL root, DB app user, Hetzner, Backblaze, registrar, Telegram bot token), both devs confirmed they can open it.
- [ ] `.env` backed up into the vault as a file.
- [ ] This runbook walked through live with both devs; each has personally run at least one playbook end-to-end in a non-destructive way (e.g., the restore drill).
- [ ] Monthly restore drill (Section 9) executed successfully with both devs present and understanding every step.
- [ ] Both devs confirmed receiving Uptime Kuma Telegram alerts on their own phones.
- [ ] All credentials only the departing engineer knew have been rotated.
- [ ] Ops Log doc created and both devs have write access.
- [ ] Hetzner and Backblaze billing confirmed on company-controlled payment method with auto-pay on.
- [ ] Firewall rules confirmed (`sudo ufw status`): only 22, 80, 443 open.
- [ ] Emergency escalation contacts (Section 10) filled in with real names/numbers and shared with both devs.

---

## Appendix A — Command cheat-sheet

```bash
# Service status
sudo systemctl status nginx php8.2-fpm mysql supervisor --no-pager

# Logs
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
sudo tail -f /var/www/app/storage/logs/laravel.log
sudo tail -f /var/log/mysql/error.log

# Restarts
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
sudo systemctl restart mysql
sudo supervisorctl restart laravel-worker:*

# Disk / memory
df -h
free -h
du -sh /var/log/* /var/www/app/storage/logs/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20

# Certificates
sudo certbot certificates
sudo certbot renew --dry-run

# Backups
rclone ls b2:<bucket-name>/db-backups/ | tail -10
mysql -u root -p -e "SHOW PROCESSLIST;"
```

## Appendix B — Key file locations (confirm/update if different in your actual setup)

- App code: `/var/www/app`, env file `/var/www/app/.env`
- nginx config: `/etc/nginx/sites-available/app.conf`
- PHP-FPM pool: `/etc/php/8.2/fpm/pool.d/www.conf`
- Supervisor config: `/etc/supervisor/conf.d/laravel-worker.conf`
- MySQL data dir: `/var/lib/mysql`
- MySQL config: `/etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf`
- Backup script + cron: check `sudo crontab -l -u root` and `/etc/cron.d/`
- rclone config: `~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf` (on whichever user runs the backup)
- Let's Encrypt certs: `/etc/letsencrypt/live/<domain>/`
- Uptime Kuma: confirm install path/port with `sudo systemctl status uptime-kuma` or `docker ps` if containerized

> If any path above doesn't match reality, **fix this document** — an out-of-date runbook is worse than none, because it gives false confidence.
